L28: # On the number of $m$th roots of permutations ^{0}^{0}footnotetext: 2000 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05A05, 05A15. ^{0}^{0}footnotetext: Key words and phrases: Permutations, $m$th roots, Enumeration. ^{0}^{0}footnotetext: Rivera-Martínez was partially supported by PROMEP (SEP), grant UAZ-PTC-103.
L29: 
L30: Jesús Leaños    Rutilo Moreno    Luis M. Rivera-Martínez
L31: ###### Abstract
L32: 
L33: Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer. It is well-known that a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,...,n\}$ may have one, many, or no $m$th roots. In this article we provide an explicit expression and a generating function for the number of $m$th roots of $\sigma$. Let $p_{m}(n)$ be the probability that a random $n$-permutation has an $m$th root. We also include a proof that $p_{m}(jq)=p_{m}(jq+1)=\cdots=p_{m}(jq+(q-1))$, $j=0,1,...$, when $m$ is a power of prime number $q$.
L34: ## 1 Introduction and main results
L35: Let $S_{n}$ be the group of all permutations of the finite set $[n]=\{1,...,n\}$. Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer. We say that $\sigma\in S_{n}$ has an $m$th root or that $\sigma$ is an $m$th power if there exists a permutation $\tau$ with $\tau^{m}=\sigma$.
L36: For fixed $m$, not all permutations have an $m$th root ([cite15†14 ], Theorem 4.8.2), however, Glebsky and Rivera [cite16†6 ] have proved that for sufficiently large $n$, any permutation has an “almost” $m$th root (in the sense of the Hamming distance [cite17†5 ]). Now, if we know that a permutation $\sigma$ has at least one $m$th root, how many $m$th roots can $\sigma$ have? Some results about this problem can be found in the paper of Pavlov [cite18†9 ] who gives an explicit expression for this quantity.
L37: Also, in the article of Annin, Jansen and Smith [cite19†1 ], appeared a classification of the elements in $S_{n}$ and $A_{n}$ that has $m$th roots, and they propose some problems related with the roots of permutations. In particular, our work is about some questions in Problem 1 of Annin et al.
L38: The main results of this paper are an explicit expression for the number of $m$th roots of any $n$-permutation $\sigma$ (Theorem cite20†1 ) and a generating function for this number (Theorem cite21†2 ). To obtain our expression we define some sets of non-negative integers that seems interesting in their own right (see Section cite7†2 ). These sets allows us to obtain a more simple expression that the expression of Pavlov [cite18†9 ]. Even more, a nice generating function is obtained in terms of one of these sets.
L39: Another classical problem consist in estimating the number of permutations in $S_{n}$ that admit an $m$th root. Turán [cite22†13 ] gave an upper bound when $m$ is a prime number and Blum [cite23†2 ] gave an asymptotic formula for the case $m=2$. Bóna, McLennan and White [cite24†4 ] proved that the probability that a random permutation of length $n$ has a $m$th root, $m$ prime, is monotonically non-increasing in $n$.
L40: See also the work of Pouyanne [cite25†11 ] for an asymptotic study for any positive integer $m$ and the work of B. Bollobás and B. Pittel [cite26†3 ] who continued the work of Pouyanne and studied the limiting distribution of the root degree of a permutation. This problem can be easily reformulated as the problem about the probability that a $n$-permutation chosen uniformly at random has an $m$th root ($p_{m}(n)$).
L41: For this problem, we give a proof of the fact that when $m$ is a power of a prime $q$, for all $j\geq 0$, $p_{m}(jq)=p_{m}(jq+1)=\cdots=p_{m}(jq+(q-1))$. For the case $m$ a prime, see the paper of Bóna, et al. [cite24†4 ] that includes a combinatorial proof of the equivalent equalities. Also recommended is the paper of A. Maróti [cite27†8 ] and the bibliography therein for related results about the proportion of $\ell$-regular elements in the symmetric group $S_{n}$.
L42: Another interesting article is due to Pournaky [cite28†10 ], who worked in the problem of determine the number of even permutations with roots.
L43: Before stating our main results, we shall give some definitions and notations. The cycle type of an $n$-permutation is a vector ${\bf a}=(a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{n})$ that indicates that the permutation has $a_{i}$ cycles of length $i$ for every $i\in[n]$. We use ${\mathbb{N}}_{0}$ to denote ${\mathbb{N}}\cup\{0\}$. It is an easy exercise to prove that conjugate permutations have the same number of $m$th roots.

L55: Now, we present our main results about the number of $m$th roots of permutations.
L56: ###### Theorem 1.

L64: Our next theorem provides a generating function for the number of $m$th roots of permutations.

L93: If $a\geq 1$ then $1\in G_{m}(\ell,a)$ if and only if $\gcd(\ell,m)=1$.

L98: ###### Proposition 2.
L99: 
L100: Let $g$, $\ell$ and $m$ be positive integers. Then $g\in G_{m}(\ell)$ if and only if conditions 1 and 2 holds
L101: 
L102:   1. 1.
L103: 
L104: Any prime divisor $p$ of $g$ divides $m$ and satisfies one of the following:
L105: 
L106:     1. (a)
L107: 
L108: If $p$ divides $\ell$, then $\nu_{p}(g)=\nu_{p}(m)$ ,
L109: 
L110:     2. (b)
L111: 
L112: If $p$ does not divide $\ell$, then $\nu_{p}(g)\leq\nu_{p}(m)$.

L114:   2. 2.

If $p$ divides $\ell$ then by (cite33†1a ), $\nu_{p}(g)=\nu_{p}(m)$. Thus
L120:  | $$\nu_{p}(\gcd(g\ell,m))=\text{min}(\nu_{p}(g\ell),\nu_{p}(g))=\nu_{p}(g).$$  |

L124:  | $$\nu_{p}(\gcd(g\ell,m))=\text{min}(\nu_{p}(g)+\nu_{p}(\ell),\nu_{p}(m))=\nu_{p}(g).$$  |

L128: There are another way to construct the set $G_{m}(\ell)$: choose any divisor $d\geq 1$ of $m$, with $d$ relatively prime to $\ell$, and define $g:=m/d$. It is an easy exercise to show that both sets are the same.

L150: ###### Proposition 4.
L151: 
L152: Let $a,\ell,m$ be positive integers. If $G_{m}(\ell)=\{g_{1},...,g_{h}\}$, $h>1$, then $\gcd(g_{1},...,g_{h})=((\ell,m))$.
L153: ###### Proof.
L154: We begin with the case $\gcd(g_{1},...,g_{h})=1$. By Remark cite37†2 , if $g_{i}=\gcd(g_{i}\ell,m)$ then $\gcd(\ell,m)$ divides $g_{i}$ for any $i\in[h]$, and therefore we have $\gcd(\ell,m)=1$ which implies that $((\ell,m))=1$. Now, for $d:=\gcd(g_{1},...,g_{h})>1$, by part (cite38†2 ) of Proposition cite39†3 , $((\ell,m))\in G_{m}(\ell,a)$, and therefore $d$ divides $((\ell,m))$. Now we prove that $((\ell,m))$ divides $d$. As $d>1$ and $d~|~((\ell,m))$ then $((\ell,m))>1$.
L155: Let $p$ be any prime factor of $((\ell,m))$. By definition of $((\ell,m))$, $p$ divides $\ell$ and $m$, thus $p$ divides $\gcd(\ell,m)$. Let $g$ be any element in $G_{m}(\ell)$. So $g=\gcd(g\ell,m)$. By Remark 1, we know that $\gcd(\ell,m)$ divides $\gcd(g\ell,m)$ and therefore $p$ divides $g$. L180: ## 3 Roots of permutations
L181: 
L182: Let $\sigma$ be an $n$-permutation. Let $m$ be a fixed positive integer. There may or may not exist a permutation $\tau$ that satisfies $\tau^{m}=\sigma$. If such $\tau$ exists, is called an $m$th root of $\sigma$. The following theorem gives a characterization of the $n$-permutations that has $m$th roots.
L183: ###### Theorem 3.
L184: 
L185: [cite15†14 , Theorem 4.8.2] Let $m$ be a positive integer. A permutation $\sigma$ has an $m$th root if and only if for every $\ell=1,2,...$ the number of $\ell$-cycles that $\sigma$ has is divisible by $((\ell,m))$.
L186: This theorem gives us information about the cycle structure of permutations that admits $m$th roots. But, if we know that a permutation has $m$th roots, we need a procedure to get all of its roots (see, for example [cite41†7 , §3.3]). The first important observation is that we can construct any $m$th root $\tau$ of $\sigma$ if we worked with cycles of $\sigma$ with different lengths separately.
L187: Indeed, if $\tau$ is an $m$th root of $\sigma$, with $\tau=C_{1}\cdots C_{s}$ its disjoint cycle factorization, then $\sigma=\tau^{m}=C_{1}^{m}\cdots C_{s}^{m}$, where $C_{i}^{m}$ consist in $\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$ cycles of length $|C_{i}|/\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$ each. Let $\sigma_{\ell}$ be the part of $\sigma$, that consist in the product of all cycles $D_{i}$ of length $\ell$ in $\sigma$ ($a_{\ell}\neq 0$, where $a_{\ell}$ is the number of cycles of length $\ell$ in $\sigma$).
L188: So, we can see permutation $\sigma$ as a product of parts $\sigma_{\ell}$, where every part $\sigma_{\ell}$ consist in all the cycles of length $\ell$ in the disjoint cycle factorization of $\sigma$. Let $\tau_{\ell}$ be the part of $\tau$ whose $m$th power produces the part $\sigma_{\ell}$
L189:  | $$\tau_{\ell}^{m}=\sigma_{\ell}=\prod_{\mid D_{i}\mid=\ell}D_{i}.$$  |
L190: And we can found $\tau_{\ell}$, and therefore $\tau$, working with $\sigma_{\ell}$ independently. This is for every length $\ell\neq 0$ in cycles of $\sigma$. Now, we need to found the admissible lengths, $|C_{i}|$, of cycles in $\tau_{\ell}$. We know that for any cycle $C_{i}$ in $\tau_{\ell}$, $|C_{i}|=\ell\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$, and we write $g=\gcd(|C_{i}|,m)$. We need to found $g\leq a_{\ell}$, in such a way that $g=\gcd(g\ell,m)$.
L191: Note that this number exists because we are assuming that the permutation has $m$th roots, and by Theorem cite30†3 and Proposition cite39†3 (part cite38†2 ), $((\ell,m))\in G_{m}(\ell,a_{\ell})$. Thus, any $g$ cycles of $\sigma_{\ell}$, $D_{i_{1}},\cdots,D_{i_{g}}$, can be combined in a suitable way (see, for example, proof of Theorem 3 in [cite19†1 ] or proof of Theorem 4.8.2 in [cite15†14 ]) into one $g\ell$-cycle $C_{i}$ for $\tau_{\ell}$ with $C_{i}^{m}=D_{i_{1}}\cdots D_{i_{g}}$.
L192: Now, to obtain all the $m$th roots of $\sigma$, we construct the sets $G_{m}(\ell,a_{\ell})$ and ${\mathcal{E}}_{m}(\ell,a_{\ell})$, for every $\ell$ with $a_{\ell}\neq 0$. L47: ## 1. Introduction
L48: Given a pair $(f,S)$ of a finite set $S$ and a map $f:S\to S$, we can associate with it a graph $\mathcal{G}(f/S)$, called the functional graph of $f$ over $S$. This is the directed graph with vertex set $V=\{s\,|\,s\in S\}$ and directed edges $\{s\to f(s)\,|\,s\in S\}$. The functional graph encodes the dynamics of $f$ over $S$. For instance, the $f$-orbit $\{s,f(s),f^{(2)}(s),\ldots\}$ of an element $s\in S$ is described by a path in $\mathcal{G}(f/S)$.
L49: Moreover, an element $s\in S$ is $f$-periodic if and only if it belongs to a cycle of $\mathcal{G}(f/S)$. One of the motivation of studying finite dynamical systems is due to their applications such as integer factorization methods in cryptography [cite22†13 , cite23†23 ] and pseudo-random number generators [cite24†3 ]. The description of $\mathcal{G}(f/S)$ has been considered for many algebraic structures $S$ and well behaved maps $f$.
L50: In many cases, the functional graphs turns out to have many remarkable properties such as regularity on the indegrees and symmetries on its cycles that allow us to obtain a partial or complete description of their structure. See [cite25†6 , cite26†10 , cite27†11 , cite28†12 , cite29†14 , cite30†15 , cite31†16 , cite32†19 , cite33†20 , cite34†22 ] for a rich source of results regarding these issues and [cite35†9 ] for a survey including some applications of dynamical systems over finite fields.
L51: When $S=G$ is a finite group, it is natural to consider the power map $\varphi_{t}:G\to G$ with $\varphi_{t}(g)=g^{t}$ (or $tg$ if $G$ is written additively), where $t$ is an integer. When $G$ is cyclic, the graph $\mathcal{G}(\varphi_{t}/G)$ is completely described in [cite29†14 ] and the trees attached to the periodic points are described by a non-increasing sequence of positive integers.
L52: Trees constructed in this way are called elementary and they turn out to be useful to describe the non-periodic part of the dynamic of many interesting class of maps such as Chebyshev polynomials over finite fields, Redei functions and some maps related to certain endomorphism of elliptic curves over finite fields [cite36†17 ]. In [cite37†5 ] the authors describe the graph $\mathcal{G}(\varphi_{t}/G)$ for special cases of abelian groups.
L53: In section cite10†2.3 we obtain a complete description of this graph for general abelian groups, mainly using the explicit description given in [cite29†14 ] for the cyclic case and using some results of [cite36†17 ]. The trees attached to the periodic points in this case (which are all isomorphic) are expressed as a tensor product of elementary trees.
L54: When the group is non abelian the power map $\varphi_{t}$ is no longer an homomorphism and the trees attached to the periodic points are no longer isomorphic and in general it is a difficult problem to describe them. The trees attached to periodic points in the center of the group are isomorphic as we show in Section cite9†2.2 , these trees are called central trees and are, in general, non-elementary.
L55: Regarding the problem of describing the graph $G(\varphi_{t}/G)$ for non abelian groups $G$, only results for special families are known. More specifically, in [cite38†1 ], [cite39†2 ] and [cite40†4 ] the cases where $G$ is a dihedral, a generalized quaternion and some semidirect product of cyclic groups are explored, respectively. However the digraphs are not explicitly determined there.
L56: Instead, only partial descriptions of such graph are given like the distribution of indegrees, cycle lengths and number of cycles. Further results of this kind are given in [cite41†8 ] for special classes of finite groups.
L57: In this paper we introduce the class of flower groups, which contains the dihedral and generalized quaternion groups, and also some semidirect product of cyclic groups. Our main result is the description of the functional graph structure of the power map over flower groups.
L58: Such description is given in two parts: in Theorem cite42†3.9 we provide a complete description of the cyclic structure and also of the non central trees, and in Theorem cite43†3.12 we provide some properties of central trees which allow us to obtain a explicit description of such trees for very special cases of interest.
L59: Our paper is organized as follows. In Section cite7†2 we introduce the basic notation and operations on graphs and review the structure theorem for the functional graph of the power map on cyclic groups. Then, using results from [cite36†17 ], we show how to extend this structure theorem for finite abelian groups. In the last part of this section we provide some general results on the functional graph of the power map on arbitrary finite groups that is further used to prove our main results.
L60: In Section cite12†3 we introduce the notion of flower groups, obtain some properties about these groups and also prove our main results. In Section cite15†4 we apply our main results to the explicit description of functional graphs associated to some non abelian groups.

L152: ### 2.4. Some results on the power map over finite groups
L153: Let $G$ be a finite group and let $d$ be a divisor of $|G|$. We denote by $G[d]$ the group generated by the elements $g\in G$ such that $g^{d}=1$. In the next lemma we consider the factorization $|G|=\nu\omega$ where $\omega$ is the greatest divisor of $|G|$ that is relatively prime with $t$. We note that if $g\in G$ verifies $g^{t^{n}}=1$ then the order of $g$ is a divisor of $\nu$ since $\gcd(t^{n},|G|)$ divides $\nu$.
L154: In particular, the tree attached to $1$ in $\mathcal{G}(\varphi_{t}/G)$, is contained in $G[\nu]$.
L155: ###### Definition 2.9.
L156: 
L157: An element $g\in G$ is $\varphi_{t}$-periodic if there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $g^{t^{n}}=\varphi_{t}^{(n)}(g)=g$. Moreover, the preperiod of $g\in G$ under $\varphi_{t}$ is the least integer $i\geq 0$ such that $\varphi_{t}^{(i)}(g)$ is $\varphi_{t}$-periodic.

L159: ###### Definition 2.10.
L160: 
L161: The central tree of $\mathcal{G}(\varphi_{t}/G)$ is the rooted tree attached to neutral element $1\in G$ and it is denoted by $\mathcal{T}_{t}(G)$.
L162: ###### Proposition 2.11.
L163: 
L164: Let $G$ be a finite group with identity $1$ and consider the power map $\varphi_{t}:G\to G$ with $g\mapsto g^{t}$. Let $|G|=\nu\omega$ where $\omega$ is the greatest divisor of $|G|$ that is relatively prime with $t$. If $h\in G$ is $\varphi_{t}$-periodic and $h$ is in the centralizer of $G[\nu]$, then the rooted tree attached to $h$ in $\mathcal{G}(\varphi_{t}/G)$ is isomorphic to the central tree $\mathcal{T}_{t}(G)$.
L165: ###### Proof.
L166: 
L167: Suppose that $s$ is the least positive integer such that $\varphi_{t}^{(s)}(h)=h$, i.e., $h^{t^{s}}=h$. Let $\mathcal{T}_{h}$ be the rooted tree attached to $h$ in $\mathcal{G}(\varphi_{t}/G)$. Set $\tau:{\mathcal{T}_{t}(G)}\to\mathcal{T}_{h}$ with $\tau(g)=gh^{t^{\delta(g)(s-1)}}$, where $\delta(g)$ is the preperiod of $g$ under $\varphi_{t}$. As previously remarked, each element of ${\mathcal{T}_{t}(G)}$ is in $G[\nu]$.
